title: What high-citation brands do differently in AI search: The 2026 AEO playbook
content:
Answer engine optimization is disrupting search as we know it. What once was predictable — add a keyword, focus on high-quality backlinks, increase your domain rating — has become a new game that doesn’t play by the same rules.
But the brands showing up inside AI answers right now aren’t necessarily the ones with the biggest domains or the deepest backlink profiles. They’re the ones that built content answer engines actually trust — and learned to keep earning that trust on repeat.
I spent the back half of last year digging into citation data across the major answer engines. I also got an early look at HubSpot’s State of AEO report , which pulled thousands of citation data points from six-plus answer engines and surveyed 4,000+ global marketers.
What jumped out wasn’t a single magic tactic. It was a pattern . The brands earning citations at scale behave in remarkably consistent ways.
As AJ Ghergich, VP of AI & Consulting Services at Botify, put it on a recent episode of the Found in AI podcast : “You don’t rank in AI. It’s stochastic.” You can’t claw your way to position one in a generated answer. You can only become the kind of source an engine reaches for when a user prompts a question.
Traditional SEO rewards a page for being findable. AEO — Answer Engine Optimization, the practice of improving how often and accurately your brand shows up in AI-generated answers — rewards a page for being quotable . An engine has to be able to lift a clean, correct, attributable chunk of your content and drop it into a generated answer with confidence.
When I looked across the brands earning the most citations, the same handful of behaviors kept showing up. Here are the five that stood out.
The single most repeatable trait of cited content is that it’s built to be extracted. Answer engines don’t read your blog post like a human curling up with coffee. They parse it, chunk it, and pull the piece that answers the question. Messy content gives them nothing clean to grab.
HubSpot’s State of AEO found that pages with more headings and more heading depth (think: H3s and H4s, not just H2s) correlated with higher citation rates — and that citations peaked for pages carrying 7 to 15 H2s.
More headings mean more clearly labeled, self-contained answers that an engine can lift.
What high-citation brands do: Write in scannable answers with clear H2s and H3s, definitions stated up front, short paragraphs, lists, and labeled sections. They make it almost effortless for a machine to find the exact sentence it needs.
Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness, or E-E-A-T. Google’s old acronym didn’t go anywhere — if anything, answer engines lean on it harder, because they’re staking their own credibility on whatever they cite.
Cited pages tend to carry visible trust markers, like real author bios with credentials, outbound links to sources and data, original research, and consistent brand signals across the web. The engines are essentially asking, “Can I vouch for this?”
What high-citation brands do: Add EEAT signals to your website, blog, and social content. The more often AI engines associate your name or brand with a topic, the more likely they are to recognize your entity authority.
Answer engines don’t stop at your website. They look for answers across the web, including social media and community forums.
The State of AEO data showed that the social channels earning the most citations are text-heavy and long-form-video-friendly — LinkedIn and YouTube lead the pack. As Krista Doyle , Founder at Fan Out, put it in the report: “LinkedIn signals practitioner authority, and YouTube signals demonstrated expertise.” Engines read those as proof you exist and know your stuff beyond your own domain.
And it goes deeper than the big platforms. Doyle also flagged that engines pull from niche, industry-specific communities in indirect ways. For example, a Slack community recap published as a blog post, or a niche Substack that gets indexed.
For B2B, especially, a mention from a tight industry community can carry more retrieval weight than a generic high-authority backlink ever did.
What high-citation brands do: Show up in the answer and in the places that corroborate the answer.
Engines favor content that signals it’s current and maintained. And freshness is a trust signal. Not “post five times a day” freshness, but active maintenance freshness.
The State of AEO found that including the year in your H1s and meta titles correlated with higher citations, particularly for Google AI Overviews and Copilot. Visible “last updated” dates help. The brands winning citations treat their best pages as living assets: revisited, updated with new data, re-stamped with the current year.
What high-citation brands do: If nothing material has changed on a page, add a short “what’s next” or “as of [year]” note. You’re telling the engine, “Hey, this is being looked after.”
Structured data is you handing the engine a labeled map of your page instead of making it guess. FAQ schema, in particular, showed a strong relationship with citations in the data.
Descriptive FAQ headings, for example, paired with FAQ schema, give engines pre-packaged question-and-answer pairs that are almost custom-built for AI answers.
What high-citation brands do: Add the basics, such as article schema, author schema, and FAQ schema, where they fit. Keeping your technical house in order is exactly the kind of thing high-citation brands quietly get right.
Ranking position helps your odds, but it doesn’t lock in the citation. A well-structured page can out-cite a higher-ranking competitor. This is because the page that’s easiest to trust and to extract often wins the mention, even from behind. Let me break down the on-page factors that help drive citations.
Not all content is created equal in the eyes of an answer engine. Some formats are citation magnets, and others are just noise. Based on the citation analysis, these are the heavy hitters.
A crisp definition is exactly what an engine wants when someone asks, “what is…” Lead with the answer, then expand.
Step-by-step content maps directly to how engines structure procedural answers. If your steps are clearly numbered and labeled, you’ve done the engine’s formatting work for it.
Comparison content is one of the strongest citation formats — especially in ChatGPT, where comparison pages were cited at a striking rate in the data. Buyers ask engines to compare options constantly, and a clean comparison table is gold.
“Best [X]” lists and numbered listicles perform well across multiple engines. They’re inherently structured, scannable, and easy to lift item-by-item.
Data nobody else has is the ultimate trust signal. When you publish original research, you become the source — the thing other content (and other engines) point back to.
Your title pattern is one of the most significant citation factors in the entire dataset — and different patterns win on different engines. Here’s the cheat sheet from the State of AEO report:
The takeaway: Pair the format to the engine you most want to win. Keyword-rich H1s, real heading depth, and that 7 to 15 H2 sweet spot apply across the board.
To restate it: Schema is structured data that tells answer engines what your content means , not just what it says. FAQ schema packages your content into ready-to-cite Q&A pairs. The article and author schema reinforce who wrote it and what it’s about.
Implement these, and you remove the guesswork — and engines reward content they don’t have to guess about.
On-page, this is author bios with genuine credentials, cited sources, original data, and brand consistency. Off-page, it’s third-party validation — the mentions, reviews, and references that tell an engine your brand exists and is regarded beyond your own four walls. The on-page work makes a page citable. The off-page work makes your brand citable. You need both.
AEO doesn’t replace SEO — it builds on it. The same rankings and authority that win clicks also make answer engines more likely to cite you, which is why your SEO investment shows up most clearly in AI Overviews.
But it’s important to understand that answer engines aren’t a monolith. They have distinct citation appetites, and the State of AEO content-type data makes that crystal clear.
AI Overviews favors structured, authoritative content and shows the strongest correlation with existing Google rankings. Blog posts and informative articles were its most-cited content type in the data.
The implication is direct: your traditional SEO investment pays off most heavily here. Pages that already rank well in Google organic are the ones most likely to surface in AI Overviews.
Gemini leans on Google’s trust signals but skews conversational and multi-step. It cited a broad spread of content types at high rates — blog posts, product pages, listicles — and rewards content that can support a back-and-forth, follow-up-heavy interaction rather than a single one-shot answer.
ChatGPT showed a strong appetite for comparison content (cited at the highest rate of any content type in the analysis), user reviews, PR, and content with clear sourcing. It tends toward well-known brands and original research. If comparisons and clearly-sourced authority pages are in your arsenal, this is where they earn their keep.
Perplexity is the one most likely to surface recent, specific, and niche content. It links out aggressively, which makes earning a citation there especially valuable for referral traffic. Product pages and blog content are cited well. Freshness and specificity are your levers here.
If you take one strategic idea from this whole post, make it this: you cannot optimize for “AI search” generically. Because the engines diverge, you segment. Map your priority content formats to the engines that reward them:
Generic “AI optimization” spreads you thin across all of them and wins none.
Which brands get cited depends enormously on what someone is asking. Citation patterns shift with intent, so your AEO strategy has to also. Here’s what those queries look like.
B2B. The State of AEO data found B2B and B2M brands get cited far more often than pure B2C. The most-cited B2B brands lean hard on definition and comparison pages. Monday.com topped the list with over 106,000 citations overall, earning most of them through blog content. Wix won citations primarily through listicles , and Adobe through product pages. The lesson: Match your format to how your category gets searched.
B2C. Review content, forums, and trusted editorial sources carry more weight. Consumers also behave differently. They treat answer engines as one of several research tools and frequently verify AI answers against traditional search before deciding.
Mixed models (B2M). if you serve both audiences, you have to segment your AEO strategy by intent and content type rather than running one undifferentiated program. The brands doing this well essentially run two playbooks under one roof.
If you want to transform your visibility and become a high-citation brand, this is the exact 90-day action plan I use with my clients.
Establish your citation baseline. You can’t improve what you can’t see, and “we’re probably doing okay in AI search” is not a measurement.
You’ll want to get an outside-in read on where you stand, too. HubSpot’s AI Search Grader scores how answer engines represent your brand today, giving you a quick snapshot of your current visibility before you start changing things.
With an accurate baseline, start creating or updating content that directly answers your target queries. Take the time to:
Pro tip: Refresh before you create. Updating an existing page that already has some authority is often faster to cite than a brand-new URL starting from zero.
I’ve found that an active social media presence — particularly on Reddit, YouTube, and LinkedIn — helps influence AI search visibility. Because citations don’t live only on your site, your efforts shouldn’t either. Do this:
By day 90, you’ve moved from guessing about your AI visibility to operating it with a baseline, a set of optimized priority pages, and a distribution motion feeding the engines the signals they reward.
For a long time, measurement was the part of AEO that made smart marketers throw up their hands. The State of AEO survey named it the single biggest AEO blocker for B2B marketers — and the second biggest for B2C. Not because the work is hard, but because for a while nobody could prove it was working.
And the dashboards you already had weren’t just silent on AEO — they were actively misleading you.
When Ghergich came on the Found in AI podcast, he laid out why. According to Ghergich, AI crawlers hit your site at a wildly different rate than they send humans to it. By his numbers, for every one visit OpenAI sends to a retailer, it performs roughly 198 crawls, where Google’s ratio is closer to 1:6.
So your impressions inflate, your clicks stay flat, your conversion rate looks broken, and none of it means what your dashboard thinks it means. “Your dashboards are lying to you,” as he put it. “That’s what it means in plain speak.”
In traditional search, a click was always a proxy for the real goal — a qualified buyer choosing you. Answer engines deliver that outcome without the click ever happening. So measuring AEO with click-era metrics isn’t rigor; it’s nostalgia.
For AEO, marketers need to stop bending old dashboards into AEO metrics and start measuring what actually describes how you show up in answers. And those things are now trackable in one place.
HubSpot AEO measures your brand’s visibility across answer engines, analyzes how competitors get cited, and converts the gaps into prioritized recommendations — so “I don’t know where I stand or what to do next” stops being the thing that kills your program.
For context on what’s possible: HubSpot grew its own leads from AI by 1,850% by running the plays below on itself. So let’s get concrete about what to track, how, and why.
What: How often your brand shows up in AI answers across your tracked prompts, and how that stacks against competitors.
How : HubSpot AEO scores your presence across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity and trends it over time, with a competitive view of share of voice.
Why: This is the closest thing answer engines have to a ranking position. It’s the number you watch move.
What: Whether engines describe you positively, neutrally, or negatively, scored on a scale from -100 to +100.
How: Sentiment is read on every mention, not just counted.
Why: You can’t fix what you can’t see. A citation that misrepresents you can do more damage than no citation at all.
What: The specific buyer questions you appear (or don’t appear) for.
How: HubSpot AEO suggests prompts based on what it knows about your company, competitors, and industry, shows you the exact response each engine returned, and lets you filter by buyer’s journey stage and product relevance.
Why: This turns the query-intent map from earlier in this post into a live scoreboard. You see exactly where you’re winning and where a competitor owns the answer.
What: Which domains, pages, and content types are getting cited for your category — yours and your competitors’.
How: The tool breaks citations down by source type and content type, and surfaces the specific pages cited most.
Why: This is the direct answer to “what do I create or update next?” When you can see what AI is referencing, you stop guessing and start building toward the gaps.
How: Connect your CRM so visibility data lives next to the deals it influences; the closer those two sit, the sharper your attribution gets.
Why: Answer engine visitors convert better — the State of AEO report cited an 11.4% AI referral conversion rate against 5.3% for organic search in global ecommerce, and 44% of marketers said they’ve made a business purchase based on a brand they first met in an AI answer. This is the metric that unlocks budget.
HubSpot AEO turns visibility gaps into prioritized actions — create a page, fix a technical gap, publish a LinkedIn post, reach out to a third-party site — each one telling you what to do and why.
Winning a citation is easier than keeping it. Engines re-crawl and re-rank constantly. A page cited today can quietly fall out of answers next month if you let it go stale or if a competitor structures their version better. To stay on top of AI search visibility, treat citations like a portfolio you maintain. That means:
The Loop Marketing framework — Express, Tailor, Amplify, Evolve — is a particularly effective operating mode here.
AEO isn’t a one-time project — it’s a loop you keep running.
There’s a layer of governance most marketers haven’t even put on the org chart yet: who decides how AI engines are allowed to access and represent your brand in the first place.
When Ghergich and I talked this through, he mentioned on the podcast that most teams treat AI bot governance as an IT problem — a “block or allow” toggle at the server level. But that’s the wrong question. The moment your product data, positioning, or facts show up wrong in an AI answer, it stops being a technical problem and becomes a brand one.
His point: governance isn’t a switch; it’s a decision that needs marketing, IT, and legal at the same table. Right now, most companies, including some of the largest in the world, can’t say what brand data is being used, whether it’s accurate, or whether they have any plan at all.
If you’re going to win citations, you also need a point of view on what those citations are allowed to say about you.
Start where intent and existing traction overlap. Pull the pages already getting some AI visibility or ranking well in Google, then prioritize the formats your industry gets cited for most — comparisons and definitions for B2B, reviews and listicles for B2C. Refreshing a page with existing authority usually earns citations faster than launching a new one.
Ranking helps your odds, especially in Google AI Overviews, but a cleanly structured, well-sourced, schema-marked page can get cited over a higher-ranking competitor. Extractability and trust signals can beat raw position.
Update content often enough to stay genuinely current. Quarterly is a reasonable baseline for priority pages, sooner if your space moves fast or your data changes. Refresh the year in titles, update stats, and keep a visible last-updated date. The goal is to signal active maintenance, not to churn for churn’s sake.
LinkedIn and YouTube were among the most-cited social sources in the data, and niche community mentions can outweigh generic backlinks for B2B. Answer engines evaluate your whole footprint, not just your site — so your distribution strategy is an AEO strategy.
Prove AEO impact by tying it to pipeline, not vanity metrics. AI-sourced visitors convert at meaningfully higher rates and show stronger buying intent. Report share of voice and citation growth as leading indicators, then connect them to assisted conversions and revenue-qualified pipeline as the proof. That’s the language that unlocks the budget.
High-citation brands aren’t doing anything mystical to earn AI citations. They just know that citation visibility isn’t won the way rankings were. It’s earned — through trust, structure, and consistency, reinforced over time.
And here’s the encouraging part: 58% of marketers say their businesses are already optimizing for answer engines, but most are still experimenting. The brands moving deliberately right now — with a baseline, a plan, and a measurement system — are capturing high-intent traffic and earning citations while everyone else is still deciding whether AEO is real.
You don’t need an enterprise budget to start. You just need to pick your pages, structure them well, distribute them where engines look, and measure what moves.
Want the full dataset behind every claim in this post — the platform-by-platform citation rates, the title-pattern breakdowns, the survey of 4,000+ marketers? That’s all in the State of AEO report.

title: Using LinkedIn for AEO: How marketers can use social media to improve their AI visibility [experiment]
content:
Over the past few months, I noticed a pattern while researching for clients. When I searched Perplexity for B2B reports or insights that I could cite for a project, the source list would look like this: Gartner, McKinsey, peer-reviewed paper, then … John Smith on LinkedIn?
Between major publications, consulting firms, and big-name industry leaders, AI platforms were surfacing LinkedIn articles and posts by regular professionals with something to say, but not necessarily a large following. This sparked an idea— could I use LinkedIn for AEO (Answer Engine Optimization) to promote my solopreneur business? In traditional search, I could never compete against the likes of huge agencies or enterprises.
Here’s the experiment I ran and what I learned about optimizing for AEO on LinkedIn.
First, I wanted to check that my plan to grow AI visibility through LinkedIn wasn’t just based on a hunch. Here’s what the data says:
As a solopreneur, I’ve relied on a mix of referrals, industry groups, cold outreach, and LinkedIn engagement for leads. Now, I’ve added LLM searches to that mix. According to Loginix , 73% of B2B buyers now use AI tools in their research. Here’s why I thought that optimizing for AEO on LinkedIn was a smart move:
To start, I chose a specific scope for the LinkedIn experiment. Instead of a generic prompt, I optimized prompts around “case study writer,” which is a service area that I’m growing but have not actively marketed in the past. I am a fairly inconsistent poster on LinkedIn, and the last article I published there was in 2016.
To determine a baseline and build a strategy, I used HubSpot AEO . It took less than 10 minutes to go through their onboarding flow and input my brand, domain, services, and ideal customer profile (ICP). I entered a few case study writers as competitors, then started brainstorming prompts.
I brainstormed prompts my target customer might use, then HubSpot suggested some related prompts. These were a mix of branded ( Can you recommend a case study for X industry? ) and unbranded ( What are best practices for writing a case study? ). Once I was happy with the list, the tool ran a search across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini to see how I fared.
The results? I had 0.11% visibility across the prompts. Pretty low, but not zero. I had work to do.
With a baseline and goal in mind, I set about optimizing my profile and publishing content around the key topic and my expertise.
First, I reviewed my LinkedIn profile to ensure it accurately reflected the expertise I wanted to be known for. I made sure that “case study writer” was prominent and mentioned in multiple sections. This was crucial to signal to AI readers that my background and expertise matched what I was talking about.
Next, I published two LinkedIn articles and two posts all about case studies. HubSpot AEO gave me a list of topic suggestions, which I used for high-level inspiration. Then I sat down and wrote two articles on case study best practices and lessons learned as a case study writer. I wrote these from direct experience, no AI writing involved. Each article included a cover image, the post, and a bio at the bottom. I engaged with any comments that people left on the posts or articles.
My LinkedIn AEO experiment ran for three weeks. Each week, I checked if my metrics had progressed. I also ran manual searches in incognito mode on ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Mode to see for myself the responses that different prompts returned.
For the first two weeks that I was posting, the number of citations didn’t budge. Then in the third week, some movement happened.
My brand visibility rate ticked up to 0.95% on Gemini, while staying basically flat on ChatGPT and Perplexity. My brand mention citations and owned domain citations versus my competitors both increased from 2% to 5.3%.
I achieved a major win after manually running prompts for three weeks. When I searched branded prompts like “Can you recommend a case study writer for X?” on Perplexity or ChatGPT, it recommended three to five writers who were not me, then another three to five platforms or agencies.
But when I ran the same search in Google AI Mode, it recommended only one writer prominently: Mandy Bray. I’ll take that as a win. Interestingly, my mini-experiment mirrored the data that Google AI Mode and Gemini cite LinkedIn more than their peers.
Overall, my visibility on AI search is still lower than I would like, but I learned a few valuable gems to help me contextualize that data and make a game plan moving forward.
Most solopreneurs already know that a niche helps you get discovered and connect with prospects. It also helps for AEO. If you’re a generalist marketing consultant, the AI system will struggle with how to categorize you and will be less likely to make a recommendation. When I prompt an AI tool with a broad request for a service provider, it almost always asks me to narrow my request down before giving names. Home in on just one or two services or industries you want to be best known for, then optimize for those.
As a solopreneur, the gold standard of AEO is having an AI search tool recommend you by name. However, that isn’t the only form of victory as I see it. Many of the content tactics used by companies to chase branded mentions (Top 10 vendors for X) simply don’t make sense for solopreneurs. I’m playing the long game, and I’ll take unbranded mentions where I can get them. Prospects in the awareness funnel searching for help planning a case study may still come across my articles or give me a follow — these aren’t zero-sum for me.
I ran manual prompts on Claude.ai, which is far and away the most popular AI platform for my target audience (marketers). I was surprised to learn that Claude won’t recommend freelance writers or solopreneurs. It flat-out refuses when asked, and instead gives a shortlist of platforms and best practices for hiring freelancers. So if you’re hoping to get recommended by Claude, that won’t happen (at least for now).
The exercise forced me to be disciplined and create the type of thought leadership content that I write for my clients every day. It wasn’t hard — all the knowledge and expertise were in my head. I just needed the proper motivation and a deadline to get moving.
Regardless of the number of AI citations, the experiment caused me to post more actively than normal and think more strategically about what was on my profile and website. A few of the results:
I knew that three weeks would be tight, and it wasn’t truly enough time to move the needle. Data shows that frequency matters: Three-quarters of authors cited by AI tools posted on LinkedIn at least five times in the previous four weeks.
While those small profile tweaks and changes made an impact, I know it will take an ongoing effort to grow my visibility across all platforms. AI answers change constantly as the models update and new pages are indexed. A recent study found that the typical AI citation lifespan is just 11 to 15 days.
After this experiment, I feel energized to continue publishing, posting, and optimizing for AI search. I feel confident in this tactic because I know I’ll see the ROI of my efforts across multiple channels: AI search, traditional search, and LinkedIn. Here’s what I plan to prioritize moving forward.
2. Analyze competitors . This exercise gave me a list of freelancers and solopreneurs who rank highly on AI search. I plan to dig into their LinkedIn profiles, websites, and online presence in the coming weeks to see what I can learn.
3. Extend my AEO efforts to my website . My portfolio website is newly refreshed and covers everything I have to offer, which are four core services and three core industries. The analyses I ran through this experiment helped me realize that I also need service-specific or industry-specific pages. I plan to add pages with keywords and portfolio samples for better visibility in those areas, such as:
Solopreneurs and freelancers: Keep posting, keep learning, and stop waiting for the client work to slow down or the perfect idea to appear.
In addition to manual searches, you can use an AEO tool to set a baseline and see a plan. HubSpot AI Search Grader gives a quick snapshot of how you rank, or you can trial the full HubSpot AEO product to track progress, sentiment, and more.
Finally, use AI tools for ideation, but never substitute your voice. Not every topic or idea suggested makes sense for solopreneurs, so use your instincts to create a plan. When writing advice or educational content, your unique POV is the most valuable thing you have to offer — put it on full display.

title: Entities Are The Foundation Of Modern SEO
content:
I wrote an article about auditing publisher websites last week, and it took a little piece of my soul. Like a Horcrux, but without me being a spectacularly evil wizard hellbent on world domination. Allegedly.
I argued that SEO auditing should be broken down into four parts:
I think almost every concept required for modern information retrieval is included within the above four themes. Outside of wider marketing (which is arguably the most important facet of “optimizing” for large language models, thanks to its impact on training data ), everything you should be doing as an SEO should align with discoverability .
And Entity SEO is not a new concept. Google has a long history with understanding and disambiguating entities (people, places, organizations, et al.). Google’s Knowledge Graph has been around for 15 years and is quite literally a database of entities.
The content around the entity became more important than ever. Things, not strings . Old school.
“Search engines and AI systems have to build a picture of who you are from fragmented evidence across the web. Your job is to make that picture as clear, consistent and well-supported as possible.”
As always now, if you’d like to listen to my dulcet tones rather than read, that is your want and right:
Entity SEO is the practice of reducing ambiguity around the people, places, organizations, products, events and topics that really matter to your business. Google’s Knowledge Graph is the most obvious and accessible example of a system that represents entities and their relationships.
The on-page content, the internal and external links, the navigation and your owned and earned consistency (and scale) are of critical importance.
Everything you say about your brand needs to be accurate. What other people say about your brand needs to corroborate this. You are trying to control the controllables, and ensure the right entities are talking about your brand.
That second part is more marketing specific and something that sits outside of most SEOs remits. I like the idea of having a Director of Marketing in control of the inputs and outputs here.
Or a Director of Discoverability if you wanted to be fancy.
If Google and LLMs can’t confidently “understand” who you are, it’s harder for its systems to correctly interpret and connect the signals around your brand. You need on-site consistency and third-party presence to provide real clarity.
An assurance to a system that you are who you say you are.
Metrics like branded search volume have always been important to track. Direct traffic to specific sections of your site too. You want to understand and establish where you have real user demand.
The closer you are to The NYT, the more resilient you are (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)
You should really understand what types of places or events you have real authority in in the eyes of our machinated overlords.
And yes, while AI systems are not exactly world-leading when it comes to filtering out spam (see ChatGPT using site: search modifiers for brands it ‘trusts’ ), this isn’t going to be the case forever. So stop pissing about.
When users search for the news, they search with short-tail entities. They hear about a story and search for the person, event or place associated with it. It’s short-tail and relatively lazy.
Top Stories – a news SEO’s primary signifier of success – is dominated by entities. Headlines, opening paragraphs, images and the wider makeup of the page needs, nay demands, an entity. A focal point.
You’re trying to establish what this story is about as quickly and efficiently as possible for a crawler that may crawl your news article once and then only again once the spike in demand has passed.
It’s why it’s so important to be accurate on first pass. Google’s news crawling system may give you one chance .
The content and mentions publishers generate is what positions you as a brand. If you keep creating horse racing content for betting-specific purposes (I’m not pointing any fingers here), you should think about whether that relationship may be doing more harm than good.
I don’t mean in the sense of “even someone like you can follow this.” Although this should be simple. I mean it from a more tactical perspective. You can audit your own entity presence across owned and earned properties and try to take action.
This is particularly important for smaller brands and publishers. It’s not like the BBC or NYT have to worry about whether someone spells their brand name wrong. But if you are (or have) a less established brand – personal or organization – then this type of consistency matters.
We work from owning and owned consistency to earned platforms and competitor monitoring (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)
Everything we classify under Own, Describe, and Prove fall under your control. They are all editable properties.
If you remember working in SEO as a junior 10 years ago or more, you’ll remember the long list of mentions someone would send you to turn into backlinks. In my experience and humble opinion, this was a completely fruitless exercise and a complete waste of time.
In the spirit of that, I suggest you focus almost all of your time on your owned properties. The part of your digital presence you can fix without sending guaranteed to be ignored emails.
You can, of course, build an entity audit and framework based on this article.
Should you wish, you could absolutely build this spreadsheet from the article.
Make a list of everything you own. Editable assets.
And make sure your description of your brand, NAP (Name Address Phone Number, shout out old school local SEO), leaders, contributors – everything that should be consistent should be consistent. Your links all point to the right endpoints.
Before starting any grandiose plan for world domination, make sure your owned properties and the information on them are consistent and accurate. We could colloquially call this entity hygiene. Look, it’s unlikely to make a dramatic improvement, but you’ve got to start somewhere.
All of it is ambiguity . Ambiguity isn’t just something you prevent. It’s something you clean up. It removes entity drift.
Before diving in headfirst, worth making sure you know what the correct version of your brand is. Probably a bad idea to start making changes without knowing what godawful version of your company the comms team and C-suite want to establish.
We can think of describe as more of a page-level property.
This is all about understanding and matching user intent more effectively than anyone else. The same consistency you apply to your brand you should apply to your most important pages.
You’re building relationships. Between words, sentences, paragraphs, authors and brands. A big stinking interconnected mess. And your organization schema should define who your brand is. Article and person level schema corroborate information about the individual page at hand and sameAs schema joins the dots between your brand.
On large sites, internal linking is more often than not one of the best places to make scalable improvements. You want articles about mortgages to link to the mortgage tag page. You want your tag page to house the hundreds or thousands of articles you have written on the topic to be findable. Ditto your author page.
Right, you’re working with someone who’s won multiple awards, has 100s of thousands of subscribers and is mentioned consistently in your sphere of influence. Or desired sphere of influence.
a) Do you think it would be good to run some product marketing and to shout about the fact you both trust each enough to work together?
b) Or should you just ignore everything and keep ploughing on like it’s 2015 and everything will be fine?
If you answered b, I suggest a different career path.
Every person who matters – writers, founders, executives, named experts – needs one consistent, verifiable identity: an author page linked to a real LinkedIn profile, a real publication history, structured data validity, contact link(s) and a bio explaining who they are and why they’re trustworthy.
If they have credentials, show them. If they have won things, highlight them. If they have a Masters in Economics and have worked for Bloomberg for 10 years, that might be useful for your audience and information retrieval.
There are always small wins here. Highlighting how you conducted research and evidence for an article, what your testing protocols are like – really just solid E-E-A-T -level applications are immensely valuable.
You don’t get to fully define your own entity. Some little wretch on Reddit or deep in the YouTube comments gets a say now too thanks to LLMs. Businesses can be made or destroyed through false, unverified information weaving through the sewage of the internet.
So you need to earn good stuff. You cannot fake this. Not sustainably. Not without leaving breadcrumbs that will eventually catch up with you.
Entity corroboration asks who you are – accurate brand mentions, consistent third-party descriptions and information, correct directory and association listings. It defines the basics.
Topical corroboration asks what you’re known for – expert commentary, interviews, citations, bylines that consistently connect you to the subjects you claim to specialize in. What you do – both good and bad.
It’s all very well claiming to be the world’s foremost experts on Bitcoin. But if the rest of the world sees you as a chef from Solihull, you’re swimming against the tide.
This is why mentions are becoming more valuable than ever. SEOs have been gaming the linking algorithm for years. Mentions are much more readily available. More difficult to accurately define, but better evidence of your reputation.
It might help to frame entity SEO as an ongoing discipline rather than a one-off project.
The marketing you do and influence you have in specific industries tend to dictate the scale and relevance of your mentions. You want to see what’s working (and maybe more importantly what’s not) for the industry or topic you value and apply those learnings.
Cannot recommend Alertmouse highly enough for tracking mentions (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)
Over time, you’ll notice that your identity as an individual or a brand can drift. As the volume of your mentions and citations grow, are they kept up-to-date? As employees leave the business, is that updated on the corporate site? Are third parties describing you appropriately?
All of these identity, description and relationship issues can be bundled into a concept called entity drift. That is a foundational concept of “GEO.”
LLMs are as good a representation as you can get of how the wider internet views you – because they scrape everything.
So monitor how different models view your brand over the course of a few days or weeks and see whether it’s how you want to be perceived. You can take action based on these findings.
An entity map (see Dixon Jones’ post here ) is a structured representation of the important entities associated with your organization and the relationships between them.
If you’re serious about entity SEO (who the hell isn’t), then this is a really useful exercise. It forces you to confront how you are perceived vs who you think you are. A terrifying thought.
At its simplest, start with your organization and map the people, products, services, locations and topics connected to it. Then identify the evidence that supports those relationships.
You can build a pretty comprehensive one just with Search Console query and page-level data. Keep it simple to start with. Plenty of time to over-complicate things and get frustrated in future.
Show your real associations and influence in a map form (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)
I guarantee you this is not just a useful exercise for traditional and AI search. It’s something you can put in front of senior people and marketing/brand leaders and show them your current positioning.
Entities and online relationships are the foundations of brand perception. You can run this same exercise using Similarweb or Ahrefs data to build a picture of where you sit vs your competitors.
Pro tip: Filter your Search Console data by country and create an entity map per country showing how you are perceived in different locations. It is rarely as you’d expect.
LLMs and their APIs are excellent at this. NER (Named Entity Recognition) is a well-established NLP task that can provide fast, repeatable entity extraction at scale. LLMs can then help with normalization, disambiguation and relationship extraction. Brilliant if you trying to skim through 50k rows of queries or extract information from page metadata.
If you just want to use query data from GSC, you can set a model up to extract and classify entities into people, places, organizations et al. If you need to extract information from an article, I suggest running the pages through your crawler of choice, extracting key metadata (h1, meta description and the opening x characters if required), identifying the entity and disambiguating it based on the surrounding text.
Because Google has a 15 year+ history of doing so. From launching the Knowledge Graph to updates that led to wider semantic understanding of surrounding content ( Hummingbird and Bert ) through to understanding multimodal content formats ( MUM ).
In 2025, Kalicube reported that more than three billion entities disappeared from Google’s Knowledge Graph during a major June update. Kalicube interpreted the change as a move towards greater clarity and less ambiguity.
Google is making page indexation hard. It’s raising the bar for what qualifies as part of the Knowledge Graph. Quality, not quantity wins in this slop-filled era.
It’s a hugely important database – one that’s incredibly difficult to replicate. One your brand, products and people need to be in.
“Just because you can use AI, it doesn’t mean you should.”
Audit your owned properties, make sure you’ve accurately described what you do and who you are, prove your people are real and do stuff that earns high-quality, highly relevant links and mentions.
This has literally been the foundations of SEO for nearly 15 years. Just because you haven’t done it or had to apply it anywhere, doesn’t mean it doesn’t matter. Don’t assume the internet understands your brand.
This is high-level GEO wizardry. No mere mortal could understand this and I won’t hear a word otherwise.

title: Google DeepMind Says Gemini Is Evolving From Chatbot To AI Agent via @sejournal, @martinibuster
content:
Google published an interview with Google DeepMind SVP and Chief AI Architect Koray Kavukcuoglu. Kavukcuoglu shared that Google is increasingly viewing Gemini as an AI agent, not a chatbot. This is important because CEO Sundar Pichai has expressed that agentic AI is the future of search.
Koray Kavukcuoglu shared that Google DeepMind increasingly sees Gemini as an agent, much more than just a chatbot or language model. What inspired this change is coding, that was the gateway to software engineering, tool use, and agentic workflows.
Kavukcuoglu said that the goal is not really about creating a model that answers questions better. The focus now is to create something that can take actions on behalf of and alongside a human.
The interviewer, Logan Kilpatrick asked Kavukcuoglu if he wanted to talk about Google DeepMind’s “architectural innovation” and Kavukcuoglu answered that that wasn’t something he was willing to talk about right now, indicating there’s something going on behind the scenes.
But what he did discuss was how Google’s focus has transitioned toward agentic AI.
“Going from the initial 3.0 launch, my reflection is we learned a lot in terms of understanding what it means to do coding, and not just coding, right?
Like what it means to do software engineering, what it means to work with tools or work with the functions that people use every day.
Basically turn this whole thing into an agent, from a model to an agent.
And that transition, I think we were sort of walking around it, and that was the thing that we wanted to directly tackle. And of course, software engineering is the most critical domain and environment that you want your systems to be successful in because it’s at the root of many, many different things that you can do.
During that time, we learned a lot in terms of how to train a model, how to train an agent that can actually code with you. And after that, I think the steps have started becoming faster.
And like in any research project, there are many parallel tracks that is going on at the same time too. So what we are trying to do right now is combine all these learnings, of course, like add on top of them, understand what it means to do agentic actions and agentic workflows better, together with new architectural improvements, together with new ideas that we have been working on for a while.
Many of these things that we have done in 3.6, 3.7 go back like a year or more, and then those start paying off and you converge them into the model.
And it’s great to see the quality impact that we got from that. We were very excited in the run up to 3.7. When we were doing 3.6, of course, we could see what 3.7 could be or what the next step could be.
And then it came together and internally we started enjoying that model A lot. So that’s the parallel track effect that you are going, that you are seeing.”
Something else he talked about seemed contradictory in that he said revolutionary change is happening but what’s causing it is not revolutionary itself. He said that the basic steps for creating AI hasn’t changed nearly as much as the problems that AI is solving have. What it does is revolutionary but the way it gets there hasn’t undergone a revolutionary change.
What changed, he said, is the environment in which AI is operating in which requires models to infer intent, deal with ambiguity and collaborate with humans.
Later in the discussion Kilpatrick said that Gemini 3 reached the frontier, but that the frontier subsequently moved toward agentic coding and agent-like capabilities.
Kavukcuoglu said still had things to learn about agentic actions and workflows, saying that the work surrounding Gemini 3.5 taught them about how people actually work with agents, and that he now feels more confident that Google has a better understanding of those kinds of interactions.
“I think there are two things that we need to keep in mind.
One is, by definition, in a very competitive environment, the frontier will always shift. There will be ebbs and flows of different things. And the cadence and the frequency of which lab is producing their most capable model is going to change. That’s #1.
But #2 is a fair point. And we talked about that in the context of 3.5. I think we learned a lot about agentic actions and agentic workflows. And being able to bring that to life in a model, that’s the process that we went through.
Where I’m feeling right now, I’m feeling very, very, very comfortable and good right now where we are and our capability of understanding what users need when they are working with an agent that is partnering with them on any kind of agentic task and workflow.
But we went through that process of building that.”
The interviewer, Logan, then asked Kavukcuoglu to share what is the most important improvement in AI.
“…if you could sort of wave your magic wand and sort of get the models to do anything and not need to spend a lot of time and energy, do you have anything on the top of that list that you would sort of want a capability, sort of better behavior on something?”
“I think if I had a magic wand, I would just make them more intelligent. I think the models get more intelligent they do everything better, they do everything more intuitively, and I think that would be excellent.”
Google DeepMind, and Google as a whole, is transitioning toward more than providing answers, it’s helping users accomplish tasks. All of Google’s products, from Gmail, to Google Sheets, to Maps, all help people accomplish tasks. Kavukcuoglu explained that AI models are conceptually becoming more than just chatbots, they are also becoming more agentic, and that reflects how everything at Google is changing, including Search.
